# What Is Probability

## A Number Between 0 and 1

- Probability is a number that tells us how likely something is.
- It sits between 0 and 1. 0 means impossible. 1 means certain.
- A probability of 0.5 means exactly as likely as not.

## Notation We Will Use

- We write the probability of event A as P(A).
- If A is "it rains tomorrow," P(A) is how likely rain is.
- You will see this notation constantly for the rest of this course.

## A First Example, Rolling a Die

- Roll a fair six sided die once. Six outcomes, all equally likely.
- The probability of any one outcome, say a 4, is 1 out of 6.

$$P(4) = \dfrac{1}{6}$$

## Two Basic Rules

- All outcome probabilities must add up to 1. Something has to happen.
- P(not A) equals 1 minus P(A). So P(not rolling a 4) is 5/6.
- These two rules hold no matter how complicated things get.

# From One Event to Another, Conditional Probability

## When Knowing One Thing Changes Another

- Sometimes knowing one event changes the odds of another.
- We write this as P(B given A), or P(B | A).
- This idea, updating a probability with new information, drives most of today's session.

## A Simple Conditional Example

- A bag has 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. Draw one, set it aside, then draw a second.
- P(first ball is red) is 3 out of 5.
- Given the first ball was red, only 2 red and 2 blue remain. Now P(second ball is red) is 1 out of 2. Knowing the first draw changed the odds for the second.

## This Idea Is Not New to You

- Simpson's paradox, from last week, works the same way.
- A trend reversing across subgroups is a conditional probability changing.
- Today just gives that instinct a name and a notation.

# Probability, a Measure of Uncertainty

## Uncertainty and Probability Are Not the Same Thing

- Uncertainty is a state: simply not knowing something for sure.
- Probability is a tool: a number we use to measure that uncertainty.
- "Not sure if it will rain" is uncertainty. "30 per cent chance of rain" is that same uncertainty, made precise.

## Two Very Different Questions

- Every example so far involved counting: six sides, five balls.
- "What fraction of flips land heads over a million tries" is a frequency question, something you could count.
- "How likely is this patient to benefit from this medicine" has no long run to count. Probability still has to answer it.

## Before and After, Two Kinds of Not Knowing

- Before a coin lands, the outcome is genuinely open. This is aleatory uncertainty.
- After it lands, but before you look, the outcome is fixed. You just don't know it yet. This is epistemic uncertainty.
- Most probabilities in this course, a screening test, a court case, are epistemic [@spiegelhalter2019art].

## Three Ways People Have Tried to Define It

- Statisticians disagree on what probability actually is.
- One view ties it to long run frequency. Another to a physical propensity. A third to personal belief, updated with evidence.
- One statistician argues probability doesn't exist as a fixed fact at all, only as what we currently know [@spiegelhalter2019art].

## Why This Course Leans Personal, Not Just Frequency

- A courtroom or a diagnosis offers no long run of repeats to count.
- What it offers is a belief, stated as a number, that shifts as evidence comes in.
- This is the idea the rest of today builds on.

# What a P Value Actually Tells You

## What Do We Mean by a Hypothesis

- A hypothesis is a specific, checkable claim.
- Most tests start with a null hypothesis: the boring claim that nothing is going on.
- Example: "this coin is fair," or P(heads) equals 0.5.

## Null Versus Alternative

- Every test also needs an alternative hypothesis: the claim you actually suspect.
- Alternative here: "this coin favours heads," or P(heads) is greater than 0.5.
- A test is really a contest between these two claims, refereed by the data.

## A Concrete Walkthrough

- Suppose you flip a suspect coin 20 times and get 16 heads.
- Ask one specific question: if the coin were actually fair, how likely is 16 or more heads out of 20, just by chance?
- It turns out this chance is small, about 6 in 1,000. A fair coin could produce this, but it would be a rare thing for it to do.

## The Logic Being Used

- The coin walkthrough is a specific case of a general pattern.
- Assume the null hypothesis is true. Work out how unlikely your data would be under that assumption. If very unlikely, treat the assumption as probably false.
- Ellenberg calls this the reductio ad unlikely [@ellenberg2014hownotwrong].

## Why the Cousin Is Not as Reliable

- A true reductio ad absurdum reaches certainty. An impossible result means the assumption must be false.
- A reductio ad unlikely only reaches improbability. Improbable things still happen.
- Ellenberg is blunt: this reasoning is not logically valid in general, just a useful habit [@ellenberg2014hownotwrong].

## A P Value Is Not the Probability You Want

- That 6 in 1,000 figure from the coin walkthrough is a p value.
- A p value answers one narrow question: how likely is data this extreme, if the null hypothesis were true.
- It does not tell you the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
- Confusing those two is exactly where the reductio ad unlikely breaks down.

## Why Unlikely Things Are Not That Rare

- Imagine a journal that only publishes results crossing the usual significance threshold, about a 1 in 20 chance under pure noise.
- Even if every study were investigating something completely fake, 1 in 20 would still cross that bar by chance alone.
- The threshold was never meant to signal near certainty, just a modest bar [@ellenberg2014hownotwrong].

# The Screening Test Paradox

## Setting Up the Problem

- A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people in a population.
- A screening test for it is described as 99 per cent accurate.
- Someone tests positive. Before doing any arithmetic, what is your gut estimate for the chance they actually have the disease?

## Thinking in Whole People, Not Percentages

- Imagine 1,000 people take this test.
- 1 person actually has the disease. The test catches them, flagging 1 positive.
- 999 people do not. The test is wrong 1 per cent of the time, flagging about 10 of them positive too.

## Counting Up the Positives

- Total positives: 1 person who is genuinely sick, plus about 10 who are not, so about 11 in total.
- Only 1 out of these 11 positive results is a real case.

$$P(\text{Disease} \mid +) = \dfrac{1}{11} \approx 0.09$$

## Checking It With Bayes' Rule {.smaller}

- The same answer falls out of the formal version of Bayes' rule.

$$P(\text{Disease} \mid +) = \dfrac{P(+ \mid \text{Disease}) \, P(\text{Disease})}{P(+)}$$

$$P(+) = (0.99)(0.001) + (0.01)(0.999) = 0.00099 + 0.00999 = 0.01098$$

$$P(\text{Disease} \mid +) = \dfrac{0.00099}{0.01098} \approx 0.09$$

## Why Intuition Usually Gets This Wrong

- Most guesses land near 90 or 99 per cent, matching the test's accuracy, not 9 per cent.
- Accuracy describes sick and healthy people separately. It says nothing about how many sick people exist to begin with.
- Because the disease is so rare, false alarms from the huge healthy group swamp the few real cases.

# Bayes' Theorem as Updating Belief

## Prior, Evidence, Posterior

- Before the test, your best estimate was the base rate: 1 in 1,000. This is the prior.
- The positive result is new evidence. Bayes' rule says exactly how much it should move you.
- After the test, your estimate is the posterior: about 9 per cent.

## The Same Machine, Many Uses

- This updating machine, prior in, evidence in, belief out, is not specific to medical tests.
- Ellenberg pushes it to its limit, applying it to belief in God itself [@ellenberg2014hownotwrong].
- Persuasive or not, the mechanics are the same ones behind the screening test and everyday reasoning.

## The One Question Worth Asking Every Time

- New evidence always raises the same question: how strong was my belief before, and how much should this evidence move it.
- A rare condition needs strong evidence to become likely. A common one needs far less.
- Probability, in this course, is a living estimate that updates, not a fixed fact.

- Next session moves this into R: simulating coin flips and dice rolls.
